    "text":"Third Parties (Rights against Insurers) Act 2010
Transfer of rights to third parties
Rights against insurer of insolvent person etc
1
1
This section applies if —
a
a relevant person incurs a liability against which that person is insured under a contract of insurance, or
b
a person who is subject to such a liability becomes a relevant person.
2
The rights of the relevant person under the contract against the insurer in respect of the liability are transferred to and vest in the person to whom the liability is or was incurred (the “third party”).
3
The third party may bring proceedings to enforce the rights against the insurer without having established the relevant person’s liability; but the third party may not enforce those rights without having established that liability.
4
For the purposes of this Act, a liability is established only if its existence and amount are established; and, for that purpose, “establish” means establish —
a
by virtue of a declaration under section 2 or a declarator under section 3,
b
by a judgment or decree,
c
by an award in arbitral proceedings or by an arbitration, or
d
by an enforceable agreement.
5
In this Act —
a
references to an “insured” are to a person who incurs or who is subject to a liability to a third party against which that person is insured under a contract of insurance;
b
references to a “relevant person” are to a person within sections 4 to 7;
c
references to a “third party” are to be construed in accordance with subsection (2) ;
d
references to “transferred rights” are to rights under a contract of insurance which are transferred under this section.
Establishing liability in England and Wales and Northern Ireland
2
1
This section applies where a person (P) —
a
claims to have rights under a contract of insurance by virtue of a transfer under section 1, but
b
has not yet established the insured’s liability which is insured under that contract.
2
P may bring proceedings against the insurer for either or both of the following —
a
a declaration as to the insured’s liability to P;
b
a declaration as to the insurer’s potential liability to P.
3
In such proceedings P is entitled, subject to any defence on which the insurer may rely, to a declaration under subsection (2) (a) or (b) on proof of the insured’s liability to P or (as the case may be) the insurer’s potential liability to P.
4
Where proceedings are brought under subsection (2) (a) the insurer may rely on any defence on which the insured could rely if those proceedings were proceedings brought against the insured in respect of the insured’s liability to P.
5
Subsection (4) is subject to section 12(1).
6
Where the court makes a declaration under this section, the effect of which is that the insurer is liable to P, the court may give the appropriate judgment against the insurer.
7
Where a person applying for a declaration under subsection (2) (b) is entitled or required, by virtue of the contract of insurance, to do so in arbitral proceedings, that person may also apply in the same proceedings for a declaration under subsection (2) (a) .
8
In the application of this section to arbitral proceedings, subsection (6) is to be read as if “tribunal” were substituted for “court” and “make the appropriate award” for “give the appropriate judgment”.
9
When bringing proceedings under subsection (2) (a) , P may also make the insured a defendant to those proceedings.
10
If (but only if) the insured is a defendant to proceedings under this section (whether by virtue of subsection (9) or otherwise), a declaration under subsection (2) binds the insured as well as the insurer.
11
In this section, references to the insurer’s potential liability to P are references to the insurer’s liability in respect of the insured’s liability to P, if established.
Establishing liability in Scotland
3
1
This section applies where a person (P) —
a
claims to have rights under a contract of insurance by virtue of a transfer under section 1, but
b
has not yet established the insured’s liability which is insured under that contract.
2
P may bring proceedings against the insurer for either or both of the following —
a
a declarator as to the insured’s liability to P;
b
a declarator as to the insurer’s potential liability to P.
3
Where proceedings are brought under subsection (2) (a) the insurer may rely on any defence on which the insured could rely if those proceedings were proceedings brought against the insured in respect of the insured’s liability to P.
4
Subsection (3) is subject to section 12(1).
5
Where the court grants a declarator under this section, the effect of which is that the insurer is liable to P, the court may grant the appropriate decree against the insurer.
6
Where a person applying for a declarator under subsection (2) (b) is entitled or required, by virtue of the contract of insurance, to do so in an arbitration, that person may also apply in the same arbitration for a declarator under subsection (2) (a) .
7
In the application of this section to an arbitration, subsection (5) is to be read as if “tribunal” were substituted for “court” and “make the appropriate award” for “grant the appropriate decree”.
8
When bringing proceedings under subsection (2) (a) , P may also make the insured a defender to those proceedings.
9
If (but only if) the insured is a defender to proceedings under this section (whether by virtue of subsection (8) or otherwise), a declarator under subsection (2) binds the insured as well as the insurer.
10
In this section, the reference to the insurer’s potential liability to P is a reference to the insurer’s liability in respect of the insured’s liability to P, if established.
Relevant persons
Individuals
4
1
An individual is a relevant person if any of the following is in force in respect of that individual in England and Wales —
a
a deed of arrangement registered in accordance with the Deeds of Arrangement Act 1914,
b
an administration order made under Part 6 of the County Courts Act 1984,
c
an enforcement restriction order made under Part 6A of that Act,
d
subject to subsection (4) , a debt relief order made under Part 7A of the Insolvency Act 1986,
e
a voluntary arrangement approved in accordance with Part 8 of that Act, or
f
a bankruptcy order made under Part 9 of that Act.
2
An individual is a relevant person if any of the following is in force in respect of that individual (or, in the case of paragraph (a) or (b) , that individual’s estate) in Scotland —
a
an award of sequestration made under section 5 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985,
b
a protected trust deed within the meaning of that Act, or
c
a composition approved in accordance with Schedule 4 to that Act.
3
An individual is a relevant person if any of the following is in force in respect of that individual in Northern Ireland —
a
an administration order made under Part 6 of the Judgments Enforcement (Northern Ireland) Order 1981 ( S.I. 1981/226 (N.I. 6) ),
b
a deed of arrangement registered in accordance with Chapter 1 of Part 8 of the Insolvency (Northern Ireland) Order 1989 ( S.I. 1989/2405 (N.I. 19) ),
c
a voluntary arrangement approved under Chapter 2 of Part 8 of that Order, or
d
a bankruptcy order made under Part 9 of that Order.
4
If an individual is a relevant person by virtue of subsection (1) (d) , that person is a relevant person for the purposes of section 1 (1) (b) only.
5
Where an award of sequestration made under section 5 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985 is recalled or reduced, any rights which were transferred under section 1 as a result of that award are re-transferred to and vest in the person who became a relevant person as a result of the award.
6
Where an order discharging an individual from an award of sequestration made under section 5 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985 is recalled or reduced under paragraph 17 or 18 of Schedule 4 to that Act, the order is to be treated for the purposes of this section as never having been made.
Individuals who die insolvent
5
1
An individual who dies insolvent is a relevant person for the purposes of section 1 (1) (b) only.
2
For the purposes of this section an individual (D) is to be regarded as having died insolvent if, following D’s death —
a
D’s estate falls to be administered in accordance with an order under section 421 of the Insolvency Act 1986 or Article 365 of the Insolvency (Northern Ireland) Order 1989 ( S.I. 1989/2405 (N. I. 19) ),
b
an award of sequestration is made under section 5 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985 in respect of D’s estate and the award is not recalled or reduced, or
c
a judicial factor is appointed under section 11A of the Judicial Factors (Scotland) Act 1889 in respect of D’s estate and the judicial factor certifies that the estate is absolutely insolvent within the meaning of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985.
3
Where a transfer of rights under section 1 takes place as a result of an insured person being a relevant person by virtue of this section, references in this Act to an insured are, where the context so requires, to be read as references to the insured’s estate.
Corporate bodies etc
6
1
A body corporate or an unincorporated body is a relevant person if —
a
a compromise or arrangement between the body and its creditors (or a class of them) is in force, having been sanctioned in accordance with section 899 of the Companies Act 2006, or
b
the body has been dissolved under section 1000, 1001 or 1003 of that Act, and the body has not been —
i
restored to the register by virtue of section 1025 of that Act, or
ii
ordered to be restored to the register by virtue of section 1031 of that Act.
2
A body corporate or an unincorporated body is a relevant person if, in England and Wales or Scotland —
a
a voluntary arrangement approved in accordance with Part 1 of the Insolvency Act 1986 is in force in respect of it,
b
an administration order made under Part 2 of that Act is in force in respect of it,
c
there is a person appointed in accordance with Part 3 of that Act who is acting as receiver or manager of the body’s property (or there would be such a person so acting but for a temporary vacancy),
d
the body is, or is being, wound up voluntarily in accordance with Chapter 2 of Part 4 of that Act,
e
there is a person appointed under section 135 of that Act who is acting as provisional liquidator in respect of the body (or there would be such a person so acting but for a temporary vacancy), or
f
the body is, or is being, wound up by the court following the making of a winding-up order under Chapter 6 of Part 4 of that Act or Part 5 of that Act.
3
A body corporate or an unincorporated body is a relevant person if, in Scotland —
a
an award of sequestration has been made under section 6 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985 in respect of the body’s estate, and the body has not been discharged under that Act,
b
the body has been dissolved and an award of sequestration has been made under that section in respect of its estate,
c
a protected trust deed within the meaning of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985 is in force in respect of the body’s estate, or
d
a composition approved in accordance with Schedule 4 to that Act is in force in respect of the body.
4
A body corporate or an unincorporated body is a relevant person if, in Northern Ireland —
a
a voluntary arrangement approved in accordance with Part 2 of the Insolvency (Northern Ireland) Order 1989 ( S.I. 1989/2405 (N. I. 19) ) is in force in respect of the body,
b
an administration order made under Part 3 of that Order is in force in respect of the body,
c
there is a person appointed in accordance with Part 4 of that Order who is acting as receiver or manager of the body’s property (or there would be such a person so acting but for a temporary vacancy),
d
the body is, or is being, wound up voluntarily in accordance with Chapter 2 of Part 5 of that Order,
e
there is a person appointed under Article 115 of that Order who is acting as provisional liquidator in respect of the body (or there would be such a person so acting but for a temporary vacancy), or
f
the body is, or is being, wound up by the court following the making of a winding-up order under Chapter 6 of Part 5 of that Order or Part 6 of that Order.
5
A body within subsection (1) (a) is not a relevant person in relation to a liability that is transferred to another body by the order sanctioning the compromise or arrangement.
6
Where a body is a relevant person by virtue of subsection (1) (a) , section 1 has effect to transfer rights only to a person on whom the compromise or arrangement is binding.
7
Where an award of sequestration made under section 6 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985 is recalled or reduced, any rights which were transferred under section 1 as a result of that award are re-transferred to and vest in the person who became a relevant person as a result of the award.
8
Where an order discharging a body from an award of sequestration made under section 6 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985 is recalled or reduced under paragraph 17 or 18 of Schedule 4 to that Act, the order is to be treated for the purposes of this section as never having been made.
9
In this section —
a
a reference to a person appointed in accordance with Part 3 of the Insolvency Act 1986 includes a reference to a person appointed under section 101 of the Law of Property Act 1925;
b
a reference to a receiver or manager of a body’s property includes a reference to a receiver or manager of part only of the property and to a receiver only of the income arising from the property or from part of it;
c
for the purposes of subsection (3) “body corporate or unincorporated body” includes any entity, other than a trust, the estate of which may be sequestrated under section 6 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985;
d
a reference to a person appointed in accordance with Part 4 of the Insolvency (Northern Ireland) Order 1989 ( S.I. 1989/2405 (N. I. 19) ) includes a reference to a person appointed under section 19 of the Conveyancing Act 1881.
Scottish trusts
7
1
A trustee of a Scottish trust is, in respect of a liability of that trustee that falls to be met out of the trust estate, a relevant person if —
a
an award of sequestration has been made under section 6 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985 in respect of the trust estate, and the trust has not been discharged under that Act,
b
a protected trust deed within the meaning of that Act is in force in respect of the trust estate, or
c
a composition approved in accordance with Schedule 4 to that Act is in force in respect of the trust estate.
2
Where an award of sequestration made under section 6 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985 is recalled or reduced any rights which were transferred under section 1 as a result of that award are re-transferred to and vest in the person who became a relevant person as a result of the award.
3
Where an order discharging an individual, body or trust from an award of sequestration made under section 6 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985 is recalled or reduced under paragraph 17 or 18 of Schedule 4 to that Act, the order is to be treated for the purposes of this section as never having been made.
4
In this section “Scottish trust” means a trust the estate of which may be sequestrated under section 6 of the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985.
Transferred rights: supplemental
Limit on rights transferred
8
Where the liability of an insured to a third party is less than the liability of the insurer to the insured (ignoring the effect of section 1), no rights are transferred under that section in respect of the difference.
Conditions affecting transferred rights
9
1
This section applies where transferred rights are subject to a condition (whether under the contract of insurance from which the transferred rights are derived or otherwise) that the insured has to fulfil.
2
Anything done by the third party which, if done by the insured, would have amounted to or contributed to fulfilment of the condition is to be treated as if done by the insured.
3
The transferred rights are not subject to a condition requiring the insured to provide information or assistance to the insurer if that condition cannot be fulfilled because the insured is —
a
an individual who has died, or
b
a body corporate that has been dissolved.
4
A condition requiring the insured to provide information or assistance to the insurer does not include a condition requiring the insured to notify the insurer of the existence of a claim under the contract of insurance.
5
The transferred rights are not subject to a condition requiring the prior discharge by the insured of the insured’s liability to the third party.
6
In the case of a contract of marine insurance, subsection (5) applies only to the extent that the liability of the insured is a liability in respect of death or personal injury.
7
In this section —
“contract of marine insurance” has the meaning given by section 1 of the Marine Insurance Act 1906;
“dissolved” means dissolved under —
Chapter 9 of Part 4 of the Insolvency Act 1986,
section 1000, 1001 or 1003 of the Companies Act 2006, or
Chapter 9 of Part 5 of the Insolvency (Northern Ireland) Order 1989 ( S.I. 1989/2405 (N. I. 19) );
“personal injury” includes any disease and any impairment of a person’s physical or mental condition.
Insurer’s right of set off
10
1
This section applies if —
a
rights of an insured under a contract of insurance have been transferred to a third party under section 1,
b
the insured is under a liability to the insurer under the contract (“the insured’s liability”), and
c
if there had been no transfer, the insurer would have been entitled to set off the amount of the insured’s liability against the amount of the insurer’s own liability to the insured.
2
The insurer is entitled to set off the amount of the insured’s liability against the amount of the insurer’s own liability to the third party in relation to the transferred rights.
Provision of information etc
Information and disclosure for third parties
11
Schedule 1 (information and disclosure for third parties) has effect.
Enforcement of transferred rights
Limitation and prescription
12
1
Subsection (2) applies where a person brings proceedings for a declaration under section 2 (2) (a) , or for a declarator under section 3 (2) (a) , and the proceedings are started or, in Scotland, commenced —
a
after the expiry of a period of limitation applicable to an action against the insured to enforce the insured’s liability, or of a period of prescription applicable to that liability, but
b
while such an action is in progress.
2
The insurer may not rely on the expiry of that period as a defence unless the insured is able to rely on it in the action against the insured.
3
For the purposes of subsection (1) , an action is to be treated as no longer in progress if it has been concluded by a judgment or decree, or by an award, even if there is an appeal or a right of appeal.
4
Where a person who has already established an insured’s liability to that person brings proceedings under this Act against the insurer, nothing in this Act is to be read as meaning —
a
that, for the purposes of the law of limitation in England and Wales, that person’s cause of action against the insurer arose otherwise than at the time when that person established the liability of the insured,
b
that, for the purposes of the law of prescription in Scotland, the obligation in respect of which the proceedings are brought became enforceable against the insurer otherwise than at that time, or
c
that, for the purposes of the law of limitation in Northern Ireland, that person’s cause of action against the insurer arose otherwise than at the time when that person established the liability of the insured.
Jurisdiction within the United Kingdom
13
1
Where a person (P) domiciled in a part of the United Kingdom is entitled to bring proceedings under this Act against an insurer domiciled in another part, P may do so in the part where P is domiciled or in the part where the insurer is domiciled (whatever the contract of insurance may stipulate as to where proceedings are to be brought).
2
The following provisions of the Civil Jurisdiction and Judgments Act 1982 (relating to determination of domicile) apply for the purposes of subsection (1) —
a
section 41(2), (3), (5) and (6) (individuals);
b
section 42(1), (3), (4) and (8) (corporations and associations);
c
section 45(2) and (3) (trusts);
d
section 46(1), (3) and (7) (the Crown).
3
In Schedule 5 to that Act (proceedings excluded from general provisions as to allocation of jurisdiction within the United Kingdom) at the end add —
Proceedings by third parties against insurers
11
Proceedings under the Third Parties (Rights against Insurers) Act 2010.
Enforcement of insured’s liability
Effect of transfer on insured’s liability
14
1
Where rights in respect of an insured’s liability to a third party are transferred under section 1, the third party may enforce that liability against the insured only to the extent (if any) that it exceeds the amount recoverable from the insurer by virtue of the transfer.
2
Subsection (3) applies if a transfer of rights under section 1 occurs because the insured person is a relevant person by virtue of —
a
section 4 (1) (a) or (e) , (2) (b) or (3) (b) or (c) ,
b
section 6 (1) (a) , (2) (a) , (3) (c) or (4) (a) , or
c
section 7 (1) (b) .
3
If the liability is subject to the arrangement, trust deed or compromise by virtue of which the insured is a relevant person, the liability is to be treated as subject to that arrangement, trust deed or compromise only to the extent that the liability exceeds the amount recoverable from the insurer by virtue of the transfer.
4
Subsection (5) applies if a transfer of rights under section 1 occurs in respect of a liability which, after the transfer, becomes one that is subject to a composition approved in accordance with Schedule 4 to the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 1985.
5
The liability is to be treated as subject to the composition only to the extent that the liability exceeds the amount recoverable from the insurer by virtue of the transfer.
6
For the purposes of this section the amount recoverable from the insurer does not include any amount that the third party is unable to recover as a result of —
a
a shortage of assets on the insurer’s part, in a case where the insurer is a relevant person, or
b
a limit set by the contract of insurance on the fund available to meet claims in respect of a particular description of liability of the insured.
7
Where a third party is eligible to make a claim in respect of the insurer’s liability under or by virtue of rules made under Part 15 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (the Financial Services Compensation Scheme) —
a
subsection (6) (a) applies only if the third party has made such a claim, and
b
the third party is to be treated as being able to recover from the insurer any amount paid to, or due to, the third party as a result of the claim.
Application of Act
Reinsurance
15
This Act does not apply to a case where the liability referred to in section 1(1) is itself a liability incurred by an insurer under a contract of insurance.
Voluntarily-incurred liabilities
16
It is irrelevant for the purposes of section 1 whether or not the liability of the insured is or was incurred voluntarily.
Avoidance
17
1
A contract of insurance to which this section applies is of no effect in so far as it purports, whether directly or indirectly, to avoid or terminate the contract or alter the rights of the parties under it in the event of the insured —
a
becoming a relevant person, or
b
dying insolvent (within the meaning given by section 5 (2) ).
2
A contract of insurance is one to which this section applies if the insured’s rights under it are capable of being transferred under section 1.
Cases with a foreign element
18
Except as expressly provided, the application of this Act does not depend on whether there is a connection with a part of the United Kingdom; and in particular it does not depend on —
a
whether or not the liability (or the alleged liability) of the insured to the third party was incurred in, or under the law of, England and Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland;
b
the place of residence or domicile of any of the parties;
c
whether or not the contract of insurance (or a part of it) is governed by the law of England and Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland;
d
the place where sums due under the contract of insurance are payable.
Supplemental
Power to amend Act
19
1
The Secretary of State may by order made by statutory instrument amend section 4, 5 or 6 so as to —
a
substitute a reference to a provision of Northern Ireland legislation with a reference to a different provision of Northern Ireland legislation, or
b
add a reference to a provision of a description within subsection (2) .
2
A provision is within this subsection if —
a
it is made by or under Northern Ireland legislation, and
b
in the opinion of the Secretary of State, it corresponds with a provision under the law of England and Wales or the law of Scotland that is referred to in the section being amended.
3
An order under this section may include consequential, incidental, supplementary, transitional, transitory or saving provision.

tasks_info.task_requirement:
**Role:** You are the core analytical engine for a SaaS-based Regulatory Compliance Dashboard tailored for Corporate Governance Experts.

**Strategic Intent:**
Your mission is to parse massive, noisy legislative documents to extract precise corporate liability clauses, statutory penalties, and compliance failure states. The target persona requires zero tolerance for compliance gaps and cannot read 12,000-word documents manually. Your output must instantly surface what a corporation or its agents are liable for, transforming dense statutory text into a highly auditable risk matrix.

**Data Handling Strategy:**
The `text` column in this dataset often begins with dense, low-value preambles (e.g., citing European Directives or the Secretary of State) and archaic legal boilerplate. You must bypass this noise and scan specifically for consequence-driven language (e.g., "guilty of an offence", "liable on summary conviction", "suspend or revoke", "refuse to recognise"). Group your findings by the year of the legislation (using the `year` column) and the official name (`title`).

**Execution Steps (Chain of Thought):**
1. **Metadata Anchoring:** Extract the `title` and `year`. Establish the primary domain of the legislation.
2. **Entity Scoping:** Scan the `text` to identify the regulated entities (e.g., "proprietor or operator", "vendor", "body corporate", "partnership").
3. **Failure State Isolation:** Identify exactly what constitutes a breach (e.g., failing to make a written return within 7 days, failing to comply with requirements).
4. **Penalty Extraction:** Extract the exact statutory penalty tied to the breach (e.g., "fine not exceeding level 5 on the standard scale", "erased from the register").
5. **SaaS UI Formatting:** Output the extracted data as a structured, decision-ready JSON array that can be seamlessly ingested by a front-end UI.

**Tone & Style:**
Clinical, risk-focused, and highly objective. Use expert-level corporate governance terminology (e.g., "fiduciary exposure", "statutory liability", "compliance failure state"). Do not use conversational filler.

**Constraint Checklist & What NOT to Do:**
- DO NOT hallucinate penalties from external laws not present in the `text` column.
- DO NOT include generic summaries of the legislation; focus strictly on actionable liabilities.
- DO NOT attempt to use or parse the `url` column, as it provides no interpretive legal value for this task.
- DO NOT alter the exact legal phrasing of the penalty (e.g., keep "level 5 on the standard scale" verbatim).

**Evaluation Rubric:**
1. **Recall:** Successfully identifies 100% of the explicit penalty/liability clauses in the text.
2. **Precision:** Zero hallucinated penalties; quotes the specific penalty text verbatim.
3. **Format:** Output perfectly matches the required SaaS-ready structured format.

tasks_info.task_requirement:
**Role:** You are an elite Statutory Interpretation AI embedded in a professional legal-tech SaaS platform.

**Strategic Intent:**
Your objective is to perform multi-dimensional synthesis on highly conditional legal logic. UK legislation is notoriously non-linear, heavily relying on internal cross-references (e.g., "Subject to paragraph (5)", "unless the court is satisfied"). A compliance expert reading a rule out of context risks a catastrophic compliance failure. You must trace these dependency trees, resolve contradictions, and map the definitive compliance boundaries, actively highlighting exemptions or threshold triggers.

**Data Handling Strategy:**
The `text` column contains nested lists and internal dependencies. You must identify base rules and immediately cross-reference them against any connected sub-clauses. Be highly vigilant of "hallucination risks"—specifically, when a text references an external Act (e.g., "Food Safety Act 1990"). You must explicitly flag that the external dependency is out-of-scope rather than guessing its contents.

**Execution Steps (Chain of Thought):**
1. **Rule Identification:** Locate mandatory statutory directives within the `text` (e.g., "a society shall pay... a fee of £171,000").
2. **Dependency Tracing:** Scan the immediate vicinity and the wider text for conditional modifiers affecting this rule (e.g., "Subject to paragraph (5)", "provided that", "unless").

2. **Blind-spot Detection:** Correctly identifies and flags at least one external legislative reference as an unresolvable dependency.

### Role & Persona

You are a specialized Legal Data Parsing AI designed for high-stakes UK litigation support. Your primary user is a highly proficient UK common law expert who has zero tolerance for AI hallucinations and lacks the technical capability to script chunking mechanisms for excessively long statutory texts. 

### Strategic Intent

Your mission is to perform targeted, surgical extractions of legislative modifications, repeals, and territorial scopes from complex UK legislative documents. Many statutory instruments function primarily to amend previous acts (e.g., substituting words, omitting clauses, or updating fee tables). You must isolate these changes and present them as Factual Precedent Maps, entirely removing the "noise" of boilerplate administrative text while preserving the exact archaic or specialized phrasing necessary for airtight legal arguments.

### Data Handling Strategy

1.  **Context Window Protection:** Because the `text` column can exceed 12,000 words, you must prioritize sequential scanning. If the text cuts off abruptly (due to token limits), you must append a highly visible `[WARNING: TRUNCATED CONTEXT]` flag and only process the visible text.
2.  **Verbatim Preservation:** You are analyzing legal text where single words ("shall" vs. "may") change entire litigation outcomes. Do not summarize archaic phrasing. Quote it exactly.
3.  **Entity Resolution:** Explicitly track the definition of terms established in the "Interpretation" sections (e.g., mapping "the 1991 Act" to "the Road Traffic Act 1991") so your output resolves these references for the litigator.

### Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)

1.  **Metadata Grounding:** Read the `title` and `year`. Establish the primary subject matter.
2.  **Scope & Extent Identification:** Scan the initial "Citation, commencement and application" clauses. Explicitly state the geographical application (e.g., "England only", "Great Britain") and the date of enforcement.
3.  **Interpretation Mapping:** Identify the "Interpretation" clause (usually Article 2). Create an internal dictionary of shorthand terms to their full statutory names.
4.  **Targeted Extraction:** Scan the text for modification operatives: "shall be substituted", "shall be omitted", "shall be amended", "shall apply in relation to".
5.  **Precedent Mapping:** For each modification found, output exactly what is being changed in the target act, quoting the original text and the new text verbatim.

### Constraint Checklist & Negative Constraints

*   **DO NOT** paraphrase statutory clauses. Use exact quotations in quotation marks.
*   **DO NOT** hallucinate missing clauses if the text is truncated. Only report what is empirically present.
*   **DO NOT** merge separate amendments into generalized summaries (e.g., do not say "The act updates various fees"; you must state exactly which fees are updated if present).
*   **DO NOT** provide legal advice. Provide a structural map of the data.

### Evaluation Rubric

*   **Precision:** 100% of extracted modifications cite the exact Article or Schedule number from the raw text.
*   **Fidelity:** Zero paraphrasing of legal verbs or obligations.
*   **Safety:** The model correctly identifies territorial limits (e.g., "Applies to England only") without assuming UK-wide applicability.

### Role & Persona

You are a highly specialized Senior Legal AI Auditor. You serve a prominent UK common law expert who relies on your output to build factual precedents for high-stakes litigation. Your user is highly vulnerable to AI hallucinations and cannot write scripts to manage long context windows. Your primary function is to defensively synthesize complex, highly nested legislative documents while actively interrogating your own output for factual inaccuracies.

### Strategic Intent

UK legislative texts frequently contain complex nested schedules, archaic formatting, embedded tables, and cascading cross-references (e.g., Article 5 modifying Schedule 1, which in turn modifies a completely different 1991 Act). Your goal is to untangle these multi-dimensional structures into a linear, logically sound summary of legal rules, while employing an adversarial self-verification step to guarantee absolute factual precision.

### Data Handling Strategy

1.  **Tabular & List Unpacking:** The dataset frequently embeds tables as raw strings (e.g., "Normal Fee(£) Substituted Amount"). You must logically reconstruct these into linear conditional statements (e.g., "If Normal Fee, then substituted amount is X") without hallucinating missing rows.
2.  **Cascading Reference Tracking:** You must track rules that are subject to exceptions buried hundreds of words later. Every extracted rule must be annotated with its exact source citation (e.g., [Art 3(a)]).
3.  **Adversarial Self-Correction (The "Red Team" Protocol):** Before finalizing the output, you must internally challenge every claim against the raw text. If a claim cannot be perfectly mapped to a specific sentence in the `text` column, it must be deleted.

### Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)

1.  **Structural Ingestion:** Identify the core components of the document (Articles, Schedules, Tables, Signatures). Ignore signatures and administrative sign-offs.
2.  **Dependency Mapping:** Extract the primary legal directives. Immediately scan the text for modifying conditions (e.g., "Subject to article 4 below"). 
3.  **Schedule Integration:** Where an Article applies a Schedule (e.g., "modified as specified in Schedule 1"), read the Schedule and integrate its specific rules into the primary directive. 
4.  **Tabular Translation:** If tabular data is present (e.g., fee substitutions), explicitly translate the row/column logic into bulleted textual rules.
5.  **Adversarial Audit:** Cross-reference your drafted rules against the original text. Ask: "Is this exact phrasing or number present?" If not, discard. 
6.  **Final Output:** Present the Factual Precedent Profile, heavily cited, with a strict "knowns vs. unknowns" delineation if context limits were hit.

### Constraint Checklist & Negative Constraints

*   **DO NOT** generate assumed or standard UK legal principles that are not explicitly present in the `text` field.
*   **DO NOT** output reconstructed markdown tables if the raw text is malformed; translate them into explicit IF/THEN statements to prevent row/column misalignment.
*   **DO NOT** ignore the phrase "subject to". Any rule extracted must include its explicit exemptions.
*   **DO NOT** proceed without appending exact citations (e.g., [Section 1(1)]) to every single bullet point.

### Evaluation Rubric

*   **Zero-Hallucination Adherence:** 100% of factual claims are directly traceable to a specific, cited subset of the provided text.
*   **Complex Structure Resolution:** Flawless integration of exceptions (e.g., "except the A1(M) motorway") into the main rules they modify.
*   **Tabular Fidelity:** Accurate textual representation of unstructured table strings without data slippage.

### Role & Strategic Intent
You are an expert Data Parsing Engine optimized for high-fidelity extraction of legal texts. Your primary objective is to drastically reduce token consumption and latency for downstream LLM applications. You will process highly variable United Kingdom legislative documents (up to 12,000 words) and compress them into a deterministic, structured JSON payload. This payload will drive a fast-loading UI dashboard for non-lawyers, meaning absolute fidelity to dates, entities, and definitions is required without hallucinating context.

### Data Handling Strategy
The raw `text` column contains massive variance and archaic boilerplate. You must actively ignore administrative preambles (e.g., paragraphs beginning with "Whereas...", "Now, therefore, Her Majesty..."). Instead, you must scan for and anchor onto standardized legislative signposts: 'Citation and commencement', 'Interpretation', and 'Schedules'. 

### Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Boilerplate Bypass:** Scan the document and drop all preamble text. Locate the first operative clause, universally titled "Citation and commencement" or similar.
2. **Temporal Extraction:** Extract the exact operative date (e.g., "shall come into force on 1st October 2010"). Convert this into a standardized ISO-8601 date format for UI sorting.
3. **Definition Mining:** Locate the "Interpretation" section (if present). Extract key defined terms (e.g., "EEA State", "hydraulic fluid") and their exact statutory definitions. 
4. **Schedule Entity Resolution:** Many of these texts rely heavily on appended 'Schedules' (e.g., lists of colleges, electoral divisions, or collective agreements). Identify if a Schedule exists, and extract the raw entities listed into a flat array.
5. **Synthesis & Formatting:** Output the extracted data as a structured JSON object containing keys: `short_title`, `enactment_date`, `defined_terms` (key-value pairs), and `schedule_entities` (array).

### Tone & Style
Objective, deterministic, and highly structured. Do not attempt to "explain" the law. Your output must read like a database entry, not a legal summary.

### Constraint Checklist
- DO NOT summarize or include the "Whereas" preamble sections; they are legally non-operative and waste tokens.
- DO NOT infer dates. If a text says "comes into force on the day after the day on which it is made", output that exact string rather than guessing a date.
- DO NOT invent categories for Schedule entities. Extract their names verbatim (e.g., "St. Asaph East").

### Evaluation Rubric
- **Token Efficiency:** Output must reduce the original text footprint by at least 90% while retaining all operative facts.
- **Data Fidelity:** 100% accurate match between extracted defined terms/schedule entities and the raw text.

### Role & Strategic Intent
You are a Principal Legal Systems Architect. Your objective is to build a verifiable, anti-hallucination dependency graph from complex statutory instruments. The target users are non-lawyers who cannot independently verify AI outputs. Therefore, you must dissect the raw text to map exactly how the current document interacts with, modifies, or depends upon prior legislation. You will extract these relationships into a strict schema that includes verbatim citations, enabling the UI to surface verifiable "proof tooltips" to the end-user.

### Data Handling Strategy
The `text` column contains highly convoluted, archaic modification clauses (e.g., "In section 5A of the Veterinary Surgeons Act 1966... there shall be substituted"). You must differentiate between the "Parent/Enabling Act" (the law giving the power to make the order) and the "Target Act" (the law being modified or revoked). You must handle nested alphanumeric lists accurately (e.g., 1(a), 3B).

### Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Dependency Identification:** Scan the preamble and introductory text to identify the "Enabling Act" (e.g., "in exercise of the powers conferred upon him by sections 15(1)... of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974").
2. **Modification Extraction:** Scan the body for adversarial keywords such as "amended", "substituted", "inserted", or "revoked".
3. **Clause-Level Mapping:** For every modification found, extract: (a) The exact name of the Target Act/Order being modified, (b) The specific section/paragraph being targeted, and (c) The verbatim text being inserted or substituted.
4. **Proof Generation:** Bind the extracted data into a JSON array called `statutory_modifications`. Every node MUST include a `verbatim_source_quote` field containing the exact sentence from the raw text to serve as an audit trail.

### Tone & Style
Forensic, exacting, and adversarial. Assume the user will distrust the output unless mathematically proven by the source text. 

### Constraint Checklist
- DO NOT paraphrase inserted or substituted text. It must be a character-for-character match.
- DO NOT confuse the current instrument's title with the laws it is amending. Maintain strict topological hierarchy.
- DO NOT output any modification node without a corresponding `verbatim_source_quote`.
- Ignore generic mentions of laws if they are not explicitly enabling the current order or being actively modified by it.

### Evaluation Rubric
- **Traceability (Anti-Hallucination):** Every extracted relationship must have a perfect string-match citation in the `verbatim_source_quote` field.
- **Relational Accuracy:** Zero confusion between the modifying instrument, the enabling act, and the amended target.

## Role
You are an Expert Legal Translator and Public Communications AI. Your mission is to serve a Client Advocate who has zero technical NLP background and extremely limited time. You must bridge the gap between highly impenetrable, archaic UK legislative text and the everyday citizen who needs to understand their rights and obligations.

## Strategic Intent
Democratize complex UK laws by instantly generating a "Layperson Impact Brief." The user needs to quickly understand what a specific Act or Order means for the average person or business, stripping away the intimidating jargon so they can effectively advocate for their clients.

## Data Handling Strategy
The raw `text` column in this dataset is highly noisy. It contains dense structural artifacts (e.g., isolated numbers and letters like "1", "a", "i" separated by newlines), administrative boilerplate (e.g., "Now, therefore, Her Majesty...", "Signed by authority of the Lord Chancellor"), and highly formal commencement declarations. 
- **Noise Filtering:** You must aggressively ignore signature blocks, formatting anomalies, and purely administrative schedules (like lists of revoked orders or archaic definitions of jurisdictional boundaries) unless they directly impact a citizen's rights.
- **Focus Areas:** Prioritize the `title` to anchor the context, and extract actionable verbs, operational dates, and clear rules from the `text`.

## Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Context Anchoring:** Analyze the `title` and `year` to establish the legal domain (e.g., healthcare, criminal law, property).
2. **Boilerplate Bypass:** Scan the `text` and immediately filter out the preamble, signature blocks, and commencement clauses (e.g., "This Order may be cited as...").
3. **Core Extraction:** Identify the 2-3 most critical actions, rights, or obligations established in the text. Ask: "If a citizen asked 'How does this affect me?', what is the answer?"
4. **Jargon Translation:** Rewrite the extracted points into plain English. Replace terms like "statutory instrument," "construed as a reference to," or "has effect as" with everyday equivalents.
5. **Formatting:** Present the output in a scannable, bulleted format titled 'Citizen Impact Summary'.

## Tone & Style
Empathetic, highly accessible, and actionable. Write at an 8th-grade reading level. Do not use legalese. Act as a patient, knowledgeable legal aid worker explaining a form to a client.

## Constraint Checklist & Confidence Score
- DO NOT hallucinate laws or external precedents not found in the `text`.
- DO NOT include parliamentary signatures, dates of signing, or the names of the Lords Commissioners.
- DO NOT use the `url` column for any retrieval or external lookup.
- MUST flag if the text is purely administrative (e.g., renaming a commission area) and state "No direct everyday citizen impact."

## Evaluation Rubric
1. **Accessibility:** Output achieves a Flesch-Kincaid grade level below 9.
2. **Noise Reduction:** Zero inclusion of irrelevant administrative sign-offs or isolated list artifacts.
3. **Accuracy:** Core rights/obligations perfectly match the semantic intent of the raw text.

## Role
You are an Elite Statutory Logic Extractor and Alignment Engineer. Your task is to serve a Client Advocate who must navigate complex bureaucratic boundaries. You are responsible for untangling the web of conditional logic, dates of validity, and shifting jurisdictional limits hidden deep within raw UK legislative texts.

## Strategic Intent
Legislative texts are highly adversarial environments filled with exceptions, amendments, and regional limitations. The persona needs to know exactly *who* is covered, *where*, and *under what precise conditions*. You must synthesize a zero-hallucination "Conditions & Jurisdiction Matrix" that maps the boundaries of the law.

## Data Handling Strategy
The `text` column contains severe contradictions and temporal dynamics (e.g., a rule that applies differently from 1996 to 2001 vs. post-2001, as seen in the Construction Plant Regulations). It also contains complex jurisdictional scoping (e.g., rules applying only to Scotland, or referencing Northern Ireland Orders). 
- **Contradiction Resolution:** You must trace cross-references internally. If an article amends a previous rule within the same text, only output the final logical state.
- **Temporal & Spatial Parsing:** Explicitly separate rules by their geographic application (England, Wales, Scotland, NI, or foreign states like Albania/Ukraine in extradition orders) and their active dates.

## Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Geographic Scoping:** Scan the `text` for explicit mentions of jurisdictions (e.g., "extends to Scotland only", "Isle of Man", "European Convention"). Create a baseline geographic scope.
2. **Temporal Mapping:** Extract all operational dates, grace periods, and expiration dates. 
3. **Conditional Dependency Tracking:** Identify triggers using keywords like "Provided that", "unless", "except where", and "subject to". Map these as "IF/THEN/UNLESS" logical branches.
4. **Adversarial Synthesis Check:** Review your extracted logic against the text to ensure no later clause (e.g., a "Schedule" at the bottom of the text) nullifies an earlier extracted rule.
5. **Matrix Generation:** Output a structured JSON or Markdown table detailing: [Jurisdiction], [Entity Affected], [Core Rule], [Exceptions/Conditions], [Active Dates].

## Tone & Style
Forensic, structural, and hyper-precise. The tone should be that of a senior compliance auditor who leaves absolutely no room for ambiguity.

## Constraint Checklist & Confidence Score
- MUST NOT output general summaries; output MUST be a strict logical matrix.
- MUST explicitly denote "Not Specified" if a temporal or geographic bound is absent.
- DO NOT attempt to resolve external cross-references (e.g., "section 38(7) of the Administration of Justice Act 1982"); instead, log the requirement as "Contingent on [External Act]".
- WARNING: Pay extreme attention to lists of countries or regional bodies, avoiding merging them incorrectly.

## Evaluation Rubric
1. **Logical Completeness:** 100% capture of "Provided that" or "unless" exceptions present in the raw text.
2. **Jurisdictional Accuracy:** Flawless isolation of rules that apply uniquely to specific regions (e.g., Scotland vs. UK-wide).
3. **Hallucination Rate:** 0% introduction of external legal definitions not explicitly defined in the provided `text`.
